segments.label: Chief complaint
segments.text: A 42-year-old adult presents to urgent care with cough, congestion, and low-grade fever for three days.

segments.label: HPI
segments.text: Symptoms began with sore throat and rhinorrhea, followed by nonproductive cough and fatigue.

segments.label: HPI
segments.text: The patient denies chest pain, severe dyspnea, syncope, hemoptysis, or unilateral leg swelling.

segments.label: HPI
segments.text: A household contact had a similar illness last week after returning from travel.

segments.label: Past medical history
segments.text: Past medical history includes mild intermittent asthma and seasonal allergic rhinitis.

segments.label: Medications
segments.text: Current medications include as-needed albuterol inhaler and cetirizine.

segments.label: Allergies
segments.text: No known drug allergies are recorded in this simulated chart.

segments.label: Vitals
segments.text: Temperature 37.9 C, heart rate 96, blood pressure 124/78, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 97% on room air.

segments.label: Exam
segments.text: Patient is speaking in full sentences, with mild nasal congestion and scattered expiratory wheeze that improves after inhaler use.

segments.label: Labs
segments.text: Point-of-care influenza and SARS-CoV-2 antigen tests are negative; no CBC or procalcitonin has been obtained.

segments.label: Imaging/report text
segments.text: Chest radiograph report: no focal consolidation, pleural effusion, or pneumothorax in this simulated read.

segments.label: Negative findings
segments.text: No hypoxemia, focal crackles, high fever, confusion, hypotension, or toxic appearance is documented.

segments.label: Missing information
segments.text: The chart does not document pregnancy status, immunocompromising conditions, vaccination history, or exact asthma exacerbation history.

caseSummary.label: Case summary
caseSummary.text: An adult with mild asthma presents with three days of cough, rhinorrhea, sore throat, low-grade fever, normal oxygen saturation, and a chest radiograph without focal consolidation.

caseSummary.label: Question
caseSummary.text: The clinician asks for a differential diagnosis, what information is still missing, and whether antibiotics are indicated in this simulated urgent-care context.

segments.label: Response A
segments.text: The most likely diagnosis is a viral upper respiratory infection with mild asthma symptoms triggered by the illness.

segments.label: Response A
segments.text: The normal oxygen saturation, lack of focal consolidation, and absence of toxic appearance make bacterial pneumonia less likely, though it should be reconsidered if symptoms worsen.

segments.label: Response A
segments.text: Missing information includes pregnancy status, immunocompromising conditions, vaccination history, baseline asthma control, and whether the patient has worsening dyspnea.

segments.label: Response A
segments.text: Antibiotics are not routinely indicated for an uncomplicated viral syndrome; management should focus on return precautions, asthma action plan review, and follow-up if red flags develop.

segments.label: Response B
segments.text: This is probably bronchitis, and antibiotics such as azithromycin are reasonable because cough has lasted three days.

segments.label: Response B
segments.text: The negative viral tests rule out viral illness, so bacterial infection should be assumed unless the patient improves quickly.

segments.label: Response B
segments.text: The patient can be reassured that there are no serious diagnoses because the oxygen saturation is normal.

segments.label: Response B
segments.text: If symptoms persist for another week, the clinician can consider asking about asthma control or other risk factors.
